This vignette shows how arimatools supports the estimation and selection of
ARMA models: coefficient tables, residual correlations for
Specific-to-General model building, joint tests and root checks for
General-to-Specific reduction, transparent information-criterion searches,
and AutoARIMA as a benchmark. The econometric theory is in the ATSE course
material; here the emphasis is on the functions.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(forecast)
library(arimatools)
```

Models are estimated with `forecast::Arima()`. Every arimatools function
that takes a model accepts its result, as well as `forecast::auto.arima()`
and `stats::arima()` fits.

## A known data-generating process

To see what estimation and selection can and cannot recover, we simulate one
realization of $T = 300$ observations from a known ARMA(1,1),

$$
Y_t = 0.7\,Y_{t-1} + u_t + 0.4\,u_{t-1}, \qquad u_t \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0, 1),
$$

discarding 200 burn-in observations.

```{r}
set.seed(12345)
y <- arima.sim(model = list(ar = 0.7, ma = 0.4), n = 300, n.start = 200)
```

The process has zero mean, so the models below are estimated with
`include.mean = FALSE`.

```{r}
fit_ar1    <- Arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 0), include.mean = FALSE)
fit_ma1    <- Arima(y, order = c(0, 0, 1), include.mean = FALSE)
fit_arma11 <- Arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 1), include.mean = FALSE)
```

## Coefficient tables

`coefficient_diagnostics()` reports estimates, standard errors,
$z$-statistics, two-sided asymptotic p-values and normal confidence
intervals for the freely estimated coefficients. Columns follow broom
conventions. No significance stars are added: in dynamic models the
relevance of a coefficient should not be judged mechanically by a p-value
threshold.

```{r}
coefficient_diagnostics(fit_arma11)
coefficient_diagnostics(fit_ar1, confidence = 0.90)
```

## Specific-to-General: residual correlations

A Specific-to-General strategy starts from a small model and enlarges it when
the residuals show dynamics the model has not captured.
`residual_correlations()` returns the residual ACF and PACF with the
individual white-noise bounds $\pm z/\sqrt{T}$ as a table.

```{r}
head(residual_correlations(fit_ar1, lags = 20), 6)
```

The same information as a figure, together with Ljung-Box p-values, is
produced by `plot_residual_diagnostics()` (see the vignette on diagnostics).
Here we use `forecast::ggtsdisplay()` on the residuals:

```{r}
ggtsdisplay(residuals(fit_ar1), lag.max = 20,
            main = "Residuals of the AR(1)")
```

## General-to-Specific: joint tests and root checks

A General-to-Specific (GETS) reduction for ARMA models starts from an
ARMA$(k,k)$ and tests the highest-order pair jointly,
$H_0: \phi_k = \theta_k = 0$, with `joint_significance()`, a Wald test.

```{r}
fit_arma44 <- Arima(y, order = c(4, 0, 4), include.mean = FALSE,
                    optim.control = list(maxit = 1000))
joint_significance(fit_arma44, c("ar4", "ma4"))
```

Before acting on the test, check the roots. `root_summary()` reports
causality, invertibility and the number of common or near-common pairs of
AR and MA inverse roots, which signal cancellation and overparameterization.

```{r}
root_summary(fit_arma44)
```

When near-common roots are present, the top-lag coefficients are poorly
identified and the usual Wald distribution is unreliable. That is evidence
that the model is too large, whatever the test says. The loop below carries
out the diagonal reduction
ARMA(4,4) $\to$ ARMA(3,3) $\to$ ARMA(2,2) $\to$ ARMA(1,1), recording the
joint test, convergence and the number of near-common root pairs at each
step.

```{r}
gets <- lapply(4:1, function(k) {
  fit_k <- Arima(y, order = c(k, 0, k), include.mean = FALSE,
                 optim.control = list(maxit = 1000))
  test <- joint_significance(fit_k, paste0(c("ar", "ma"), k))
  data.frame(
    model = sprintf("ARMA(%d,%d)", k, k),
    wald = round(test[["Wald statistic"]], 3),
    p.value = round(test[["P-value"]], 4),
    converged = fit_k$code == 0,
    near_common = root_summary(fit_k)[["Near-common root pairs"]]
  )
})
do.call(rbind, gets)
```

Summaries such as `joint_significance()` and `root_summary()` return named
lists that print as two columns; individual entries are extracted with `[[`,
as above, and `as.data.frame()` turns them into tables.

## Information-criterion order search

`order_search()` estimates every ARIMA$(p,d,q)$ in a grid and reports the
log likelihood and all four information criteria,

$$
\text{AIC} = -2\log L + 2k,\quad
\text{AICc} = \text{AIC} + \frac{2k(k+1)}{n-k-1},\quad
\text{BIC} = -2\log L + k\log n,\quad
\text{HQIC} = -2\log L + 2k\log\log n,
$$

where $k$ counts the free coefficients plus the innovation variance. Every
model is reported, including any that failed or did not converge.

```{r}
search <- order_search(y, p_max = 3, q_max = 3, criterion = "BIC",
                       include.constant = FALSE)
head(search[, c("model", "k", "loglik", "AIC", "BIC", "converged", "status")])
```

`order_search()` estimates and reports; only `select_model()` chooses.

```{r}
select_model(search, criterion = "BIC")
select_model(search, criterion = "AIC")
```

The minimum-criterion model is the one preferred by that criterion within
the candidate set. It is not automatically adequate, and in a finite sample
it need not be the DGP.

### Choose $d$ first

Information criteria are comparable only among models with the same order
of differencing, because differencing changes the effective sample. A grid
over several $d$ is allowed for inspection, but `select_model()` then needs
to be told which $d$ to select within:

```{r}
#| error: true
grid_d <- order_search(y, p_max = 1, q_max = 1, d_min = 0, d_max = 1)
select_model(grid_d)
select_model(grid_d, d = 0)
```

## AutoARIMA as a benchmark

`auto_arima()` is a thin wrapper around `forecast::auto.arima()` with the
course defaults: nonseasonal models, BIC, and exact likelihoods during the
search. Here $d$ is fixed at zero, as in the grid above.

```{r}
auto <- auto_arima(y, criterion = "BIC", d = 0, max_p = 4, max_q = 4)
auto_arima_summary(auto)
```

The result is an ordinary fitted `Arima` object, so every other arimatools
function accepts it directly, e.g. `coefficient_diagnostics(auto)`.

## Comparing estimated models

`compare_models()` collects likelihoods and criteria for fitted models, and
records each model's estimation sample.

```{r}
cmp <- compare_models(fit_ar1, fit_ma1, fit_arma11,
                      names = c("AR(1)", "MA(1)", "ARMA(1,1)"))
cmp[, c("model", "k", "loglik", "AIC", "BIC", "start", "end")]
select_model(cmp, "BIC")
```

`select_model()` refuses to compare models fitted to different observations,
such as different sample windows or a series and its logarithm:

```{r}
#| error: true
z <- ts(50 + cumsum(rnorm(120, 0.3)), start = c(1990, 1), frequency = 4)
select_model(compare_models(level = Arima(z, c(1, 1, 0)),
                            log = Arima(log(z), c(1, 1, 0))))
```

## How often does a strategy find the DGP?

Whether a strategy recovered ARMA(1,1) in one realization is partly luck.
The functions above can be combined in a Monte Carlo experiment that counts
how often each criterion selects the true model. The code is shown but not
run here, since it takes a few minutes.

```{r}
#| eval: false
pick <- function(T_obs) {
  y <- arima.sim(model = list(ar = 0.7, ma = 0.4), n = T_obs, n.start = 200)
  grid <- suppressWarnings(order_search(y, p_max = 3, q_max = 3,
                                        include.constant = FALSE))
  sapply(c("BIC", "AIC"), function(cr) {
    best <- select_model(grid, criterion = cr)
    sprintf("ARMA(%d,%d)", best$p, best$q)
  })
}
set.seed(2026)
picks <- t(replicate(300, pick(100)))
colMeans(picks == "ARMA(1,1)")   # share of realizations selecting the DGP
```

Selecting a candidate is not the end of model building: the selected model
must still be diagnosed. That is the subject of
`vignette("diagnostics", package = "arimatools")`.
